messages.subject: Fixing states at multiple nodes
messages.subject_clean: Fixing states at multiple nodes
messages.body_plain:
Dear BioGeoBEARS users,

I have added the capability to fix the state likelihoods at
more than one node, for both regular and stratified
analyses. This allows the calculation of data likelihoods
under hypotheses that certain ancestral nodes had certain
ranges.

Instead of just listing 1 node in fixnode, you can do
multiple nodes, e.g. BioGeoBEARS_run_object$fixnode =
c(20,21), and BioGeoBEARS_run_object$fixlikes can now take a
matrix with a number of rows equal to the length of fixnode.
Various other minor improvements in fixnodes analysis were
also added. To enable the improvements, source the latest
code via:

================================
library(BioGeoBEARS)
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_stratified_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_univ_model_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_plots_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_readwrite_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wikidot.com/local--files/biogeobears/calc_loglike_sp_v01.R")
calc_loglike_sp = compiler::cmpfun(calc_loglike_sp_prebyte)
================================

Yes, I will eventually put all these upgrades on CRAN, but
that is a big enough project I am going to wait until I get
all of my major fixes and documentation improvements etc.
together.

Cheers!
Nick

On Friday, January 31, 2014 2:13:00 PM UTC-5, Nick Matzke wrote:
On Fri, Jan 31, 2014 at 9:59 AM, someone wrote:

> Hi Nick,
>
> I have been playing around with BioGeoBears and I have questions for you
> about the j parameter.  It seems as if maybe I don't understand fully what
> you've done, maybe because your papers aren't out yet, or maybe I just can't
> wrap my head around it.
>
> Won't the DEC+j always be favored over the DEC because to get a 'founder
> event' in DEC you need to infer two events (anagenetic dispersal plus
> cladogenesis), versus the single event that DEC+j infers from the founder
> event?
>
> Also, I understand the d and e values from the global optimization because
> they are based on branch lengths, changes over unit time, but what does the
> j value of the global optimization mean, what does it represent? Is it the
> probability of a founder event per node, so its not a rate, right?
>
> Thanks for the feedback and take care!

Hi!

j, and the other parameters y, s, and v (usually hidden) are the
"per-event weights".  If j=y=s=v =1, then all of the events have equal
weight, on a per-event basis.  In DEC+J, j ranges from 0-3, and y,s,v
each have weight (3-j)/3.

The tricky bit is that there are different possible numbers of events,
conditional on each different ancestral range.

Basically, though, the weights get added up and divided by the total
to produce the conditional probability of any particular event
conditional on any particular ancestral range.

It makes more sense if you see it in Excel:

Go to my Ph.D. page:

https://googledrive.com/host/0B6HJElw5txrwZlhjQ0ZUcEdzUG8/2013-08-10_matzke_PhD.html

..And then the excel file here:

Supplementary Data 1: Excel spreadsheet demonstrating the cladogenesis
calculations for DEC and DEC+J by hand: PDF caption -- Excel file

Cheers!
Nick

On 2/7/14 4:32 AM, VIEU Julien wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> following the logic from the first message, the DIVAlike
> should often ( depends on max numer of areas allowed) be
> favoured over the DEC, because to infer a widespread
> vicariance in the DEC you need to infer two events: a
> cladogenetic vicariance (narrow) plus an anagenetic
> dispersal.
>
> Am I right here?

This would all depend on the data configuration at the tips.
  If you had lots of (AB, CD) species pairs, I believe these
would uniquely favor DIVALIKE.  But if there were many pairs
of (AB, C), this would be just as well explained by DEC,
which allows narrow vicariance but not widespread
vicariance. DEC might even do better than DIVALIKE at this
second data configuration, since the conditional
probabilities would be spread over fewer possible
cladogenesis events.

Intuitions about counting events will only get you so far,
since what really counts is the probability of the events
(and nonevents!) as specified by the parameters, so the
safest thing is to run it and check it.

Cheers!
Nick

Hi! So, it's hard for me to diagnose without the input files.  Typically this is some kind of precision issue where a probability which should be zero gets calculated as negative, or something like that.

If it's really true that you "change those two randomly resolved branches' lengths from 0 to 1.0e-16 (approximately twice as small as the smallest real branch in my tree)"...a branch length of 1.0e-16, or even twice that, is super-super short, and some probability calculation on that short branch may be producing an error.  I would put your tree in a timescale of millions of years, and make the shortest branch only, say, 0.01 million years, and try that.

The next step is to modify the "min" and "max" for your free parameters, especially to move the minimum further away from zero...

Cheers!
Nick

> titlecex=0.5,

>                             tipranges=tipranges)

These are pie charts of states (states = geographic ranges),
not just areas.  For 3 areas, A,B,C, you have 8 possible
states/ranges:

null
A
B
C
AB
AC
BC
ABC

BioGeoBEARS has a default color scheme where the single-area
ranges get pure colors and the combination ranges get mixes
of those pure colors.  The range of "everywhere" (here, ABC)
always gets white.

This is probably not the best color scheme imaginable but
displaying more than a few states on a plot is just
difficult.  Mostly the point of the pie charts is for
readers to see how confident / unconfident the most-probable
state at the node is.  If you have a highly-divided pie
chart then even the most-probable state might still be
unlikely to be the true one, and you just have uncertainty
at that node.

And to see if there are ties, because if 2 states/ranges
have the same probability, BioGeoBEARS just picks the first
in the states list as the one to show on the
single-most-probable range chart.

> #Using this code I get values that are numbered in various
> combinations between 0-5 but my number of states is 1-6.
>
> state_indices_0based =
> rcpp_areas_list_to_states_list(areas=areas,
> maxareas=res$inputs$max_range_size, include_null_range=TRUE)
> state_indices_0based

This is what the "0-based" part means.  Some computer
languages count indices starting from 0 (like C++), some
from 1 (like R), since I use both R and C++ in BioGeoBEARS,
I have to go back and forth.  Just add 1 to convert, if needed.

> #For the node labels there are also corner labels, how do I
> interpret that (see attached image)?
>

BioGeoBEARS uses the corners to display the ranges in the
moment just after speciation.  A widespread range might
split up (ABC -> A, BC) or you might have a founder-event
(A->A,B) or whatever.

These are cladogenetic models of range evolution.  Such
models are rare in most of phylogenetics but common in
biogeography.  See the LAGRANGE DEC method by Ree et al.
2005, Ree & Smith 2008, and my summary at:

http://www.escholarship.org/uc/item/44j7n141

And the review by Ronquist & Sanmartin in AREES.

Nick

Hi Sam,

OK I found 2 issues. One was the tree thing, I pruned the tree myself but I could have used your pruned tree.

The other problem was that the branches on your tree are all extremely short.  BioGeoBEARS defaults assume that branches are in millions of years.  Your tree has many branches of length, say, 1e-6, which BioGeoBEARS thinks of as one calendar year.

This can cause 2 problems:

1. Precision issues and underflow problems

2. BioGeoBEARS assumes by default that branches of length shorter than 0.000001 are "direct ancestors" rather than side-branches, and changes the calculations accordingly.  This was done so that I could experiment with putting in fossil ranges in rare cases they are known (this could not be done with e.g. LAGRANGE).  The cladogenesis model is "turned off" for these branching points.

This default can be changed, but it's easier to multiply all your branches by 1,000,000, which I believe I suggested before.  I've done it here, saved to a new Newick file, and it all works...

In the attached script, search on "NJM_EDIT" to see the parts where I changed things or fixed your tree.

Also, you have 3 areas, so make sure that:

max_range_size = 3

...in the script.

messages.subject_clean: "Function returned is infinite or NA" in bears_2param_standard_fast
messages.body_plain:
Hi BioGeoBEARS users,

I'm posting another answer on "Function returned is infinite or NA", so that it is easier to google up the solution.

X reports an problem with "Function returned is infinite or NA" -- this is typically a problem with the optim() or optimx() search trying some value (such as 0 or a tiny negative value) that results in an impossible probability (0, negative, or Infinite).  I have not been able to figure out a solution that works in all cases, since it is difficult to figure out exactly what values optim() and optimx() are trying during a maximum likelihood (ML) search.

However, the solution, which always seems to eventually work, is to narrow the min/max values allowed during optimization, as follows:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/biogeobears/%5B%22max%22/biogeobears/kmbkmfXzGSg/cTi_jAh78t4J
==============
Just as you can access the variable type for "j", the
initial starting value of "j", etc., like this:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","type"]
= "free"

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","init"]
= 0.01

...you can access the "min" and "max" for "j" (or "d", "e",
whatever), like this:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","min"]

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","max"]

Often, narrowing the limits a teeny bit fixes NaN/Inf
problems during the ML search.

You can access the full parameters table with:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table
==============

Also: everyone should use bears_optim_run(BioGeoBEARS_run_object) instead of bears_2param_standard_fast(), bears_3param_standard_fast(), etc.  The latter have fixed defaults for the min and max of each parameter.  They were designed just as shortcuts, but are inflexible and will be cut in the next big update.

Cheers,
Nick

keydf

keydf2

areanames

areanames

statenames

dev.off()

Hi,

Yes, this is in the example script already.

Basically, bears_optim_run() takes BioGeoBEARS_run_object as an input.  All the run settings and model settings are stored in BioGeoBEARS_run_object.

You can see everything by typing:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table

To see the current setting for maximum range size:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$max_range_size

To change it:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$max_range_size = 3
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$max_range_size = 4

...etc...

To see the influence of the number of areas on the number of ranges:

numstates_from_numareas(numareas=9, maxareas=9, include_null_range=TRUE)
numstates_from_numareas(numareas=9, maxareas=8, include_null_range=TRUE)
numstates_from_numareas(numareas=9, maxareas=7, include_null_range=TRUE)
numstates_from_numareas(numareas=9, maxareas=6, include_null_range=TRUE)

...etc...

BioGeoBEARS gets very slow once you are up to >500 states, due to the size of the transition rate matrix, which must be exponentiated by rexpokit.

Cheers!
Nick

Howdy X...yeah, BioGeoBEARS has functions for reading the various outputs of python LAGRANGE, C++ LAGRANGE, and DIVA, and plotting them in R.  It is more interesting, though to compare models.  For this data, it appears that DEC+J, DIVA+J, and BAYAREA+J all beat Lagrange's DEC by a lot.  See next email...

Below, I've pasted the script that reads in and plots the Python LAGRANGE output to a PDF in R.  PDF, script, etc. attached.  You will have to change the working directory ("wd") to wherever you save the files to make it work for you.

plot_LGpy_result_v1.R
=================
library(ape)
library(optimx)  # (either 2012 or 2013 version, as of January 2014)
library(FD)        # for FD::maxent() (make sure this is up-to-date)
library(snow)     # (if you want to use multicore functionality; prob. better than library(parallel))
library(BioGeoBEARS)
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_univ_model_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_plots_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_readwrite_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wikidot.com/local--files/biogeobears/calc_loglike_sp_v01.R")
calc_loglike_sp = compiler::cmpfun(calc_loglike_sp_prebyte)    # crucial to fix bug in uppass calculations

# Setup
#wd = "/Dropbox/_njm/__packages/BioGeoBEARS_setup/inst/extdata/examples/AAAB_M0_BL1/LGpy/"

wd = "/drives/Dropbox/_njm/__packages/BioGeoBEARS_setup/z_help/X/"
setwd(wd)

#######################################################
# Parse Python LAGRANGE output
#######################################################

states_fn = "YuleUCLD-enforced-3areas.results.txt"

sumstats = parse_lagrange_python_output(outfn=states_fn, outputfiles=TRUE, results_dir=getwd(), new_splits_fn=TRUE, new_states_fn=FALSE, filecount=0, append=TRUE)
sumstats

splits_table_fn = "YuleUCLD-enforced-3areas.results_splits00001.txt"
moref(splits_table_fn)

LGpy_splits = LGpy_splits_fn_to_table(splits_fn=splits_table_fn)
LGpy_splits

MLsplits = LGpy_MLsplit_per_node(splits=LGpy_splits)
MLsplits

# Plot LGpy node numbers
trfn = "tree.newick"
tr = read.tree(trfn)
ntips = length(tr$tip.label)
Rnodenums = (ntips+1):(ntips+tr$Nnode)

# Nodenums for Python Lagrange
downpass_node_matrix = get_lagrange_nodenums(tr)
downpass_node_matrix

# Nodenums for Python Lagrange include
# tip numbers N0 - N(ntips-1)
# E.g. in this example they start at node N4
downpass_node_matrix[,2] = downpass_node_matrix[,2] + ntips - 1

# Sort in LAGRANGE node order
downpass_node_matrix = downpass_node_matrix[order(downpass_node_matrix[,2]),]

# Sort MLsplits the same way
MLsplits = MLsplits[order(MLsplits$nodenum_LGpy),]

# Get tip states
geogfn = "geog.data"
tipranges = getranges_from_LagrangePHYLIP(geogfn)
tipranges

tip_areastrings = tipranges_to_area_strings(tipranges=tipranges, areaabbr=NULL)
tip_areastrings

pdffn = "LGpy_plots_v1.pdf"
pdf(pdffn, height=11, width=8.5)
par(mfrow=c(2,1))

plot(tr, show.tip.label=TRUE, label.offset=0.1)
axisPhylo()
nodelabels(node=Rnodenums, text=Rnodenums)
tiplabels(tip=1:ntips, text=1:ntips)
title("Tree with APE node numbers")

plot(tr, show.tip.label=TRUE)
axisPhylo()
nodelabels(node=downpass_node_matrix[,1], text=downpass_node_matrix[,2])
#tiplabels()
title("Tree with Python LAGRANGE node numbers")

plot(tr, show.tip.label=TRUE, label.offset=0.1)
axisPhylo()
nodelabels(node=downpass_node_matrix[,1], text=MLsplits$splits)
tiplabels(text=tip_areastrings, tip=1:ntips)
title("Python LAGRANGE most probable splits")

plot(tr, show.tip.label=TRUE, label.offset=0.1)
axisPhylo()
nodelabels(node=downpass_node_matrix[,1], pie=MLsplits$relprob)
tiplabels(text=tip_areastrings, tip=1:ntips)
title("Python LAGRANGE state probabilities\n(P(best state), then all others)")

dev.off()
cmdstr = paste("open ", pdffn, sep="")
system(cmdstr)
